title: Are We Facing the Worst Generation of Parents?
author: Andrew Old
summary: Responding to a Telegraph article by MAT CEO Sir John Townsley describing "a generation of the worst parents," Andrew Old is sceptical of the framing but agrees a significant minority of ideologically motivated parents now undermine school discipline more consistently than in past decades. Rather than accept Townsley's explanation that these parents simply learned permissiveness from their own parents (which he notes leads to infinite regress), Old traces the pattern to a specific ideology he calls "blamelessness," documented on his blog since 2008: a belief that children are inherently blameless, so any misbehaviour must be explained away by age, background, or a medical/psychological condition. He argues today's most combative parents were themselves educated in English secondary schools in the 2000s under this ideology, when Ofsted and local authorities actively enforced it, and that its legacy persists today in reframed language around "regulating" rather than sanctioning behaviour.
points: Old's central historical claim is specific and falsifiable: the parents most resistant to school discipline today were themselves educated under an actively Ofsted-and-local-authority-enforced "blamelessness" ideology in English secondary schools in the 2000s.

He identifies three stock explanations used under that ideology to excuse student misbehaviour -- age, background, or a medical/psychological condition -- and argues they were treated as near-universal rather than as the rare exceptions they actually are.

Old is careful to reject infinite-regress explanations (parents were simply parented permissively by their own parents), instead locating the mechanism in a specific, datable institutional ideology that has since receded from Ofsted enforcement but not from public discourse.

He identifies the ideology's current descendant as the language of student "regulation" rather than sanction, still promoted on INSET days and by SENDCOs even though most secondary headteachers, he argues, have moved away from it.
quotes: Though thankfully they remain a significant minority, the impact of those parents is profound. Theirs is a world in which their children can do no wrong and where their children’s disruptive conduct is defended at every turn.
In a post entitled Blamelessness, written in 2008, I described a philosophy based on the idea that children are natural saints.

It was necessary to come up with imaginative explanations of why children are not responsible for their behaviour, thereby allowing them to be innocent victims even when they are observed to be behaving like complete bastards.
This philosophy declined in influence (at least in secondary schools) once Ofsted and Local Authorities were no longer enforcing it.
The latest version of it is the one in which badly behaved children are described as needing opportunities to 'regulate' rather than sanctions.
Many of today's teenagers have parents who attended school in the 2000s. This is the era described in the early posts on my blog.
